summary: Allows TCP to start with a larger initial congestion window, up to roughly 4 kilobytes instead of one segment. It discusses the benefits and drawbacks, experiments showing no congestion collapse, and implementation advice. It replaces RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP may begin a connection with more data in flight than the earlier one-or-two-segment limit allowed. This can reduce waiting for short transfers, while TCP still returns to a one-segment window after a loss timeout.

subtitle: A larger optional TCP starting window can reduce delays for short transfers.

tldr.problem: A TCP connection that starts with a very small congestion window can spend extra round trips sending short transfers, especially on long-delay paths.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC permits an initial window up to min(4*MSS, max(2*MSS, 4380 bytes)). It changes the starting window, not the one-segment loss window.
tldr.outcome: The larger initial window is optional. The RFC discusses possible burst losses and reports that its studies found no congestion-collapse danger; it obsoletes RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581.

today: RFC 3390 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2002. It obsoletes RFC 2414 and updates RFC 2581; the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Initial Window Limit
sections.content:
RFC 3390 raises the permitted upper bound for TCP's initial congestion window to min(4*MSS, max(2*MSS, 4380 bytes)), where MSS is the maximum segment size. In most cases the bound is roughly 4K bytes, though the permitted two-segment window can exceed that when MSS is large.

The change is optional. It applies to data sent in the first round-trip time after the three-way handshake; the SYN and SYN/ACK exchange does not raise the window above the bound. If the SYN or SYN/ACK is lost, the sender MUST use one segment of MSS bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP can send more data at the start of a connection, up to a bound based on the segment size. The RFC makes this choice optional and keeps the loss window at one segment.

sections.title: What Changes and What Does Not
sections.content:
The new limit applies to the initial window only. TCP may also use slow start when restarting after an idle period or after a retransmission timeout; the loss window MUST remain one segment of MSS bytes.

When Path MTU Discovery finds that the segment size is too large, the congestion window SHOULD be reduced in proportion to the old and new segment sizes. The RFC also warns against opening many simultaneous browser connections to gain the effect repeatedly and points to persistent connections and pipelining as an alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the first window changes. After a retransmission timeout, TCP still uses a one-segment loss window.

sections.title: Why a Larger Start Can Help
sections.content:
With a one-segment initial window, a receiver using delayed acknowledgments may wait for a timer before acknowledging. With at least two segments, it can acknowledge after the second data segment arrives.

For transfers under 4K bytes, such as many email or web-page transfers described in the RFC, the larger initial window can reduce transfer time to one round-trip time. Connections on high-bandwidth, long-delay paths can also avoid up to three round trips and a delayed-ack timeout during initial slow start.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger first window can let a short transfer finish in fewer round trips. It can also shorten the initial slow-start phase on paths with long delays.

sections.title: Burst Loss and Network Effects
sections.content:
A burst of initial segments may be dropped by a congested router, especially one using a Drop Tail queue. A connection starting with one segment might avoid a loss that affects a larger first burst.

The RFC examines two possible network effects: duplicate segments and segments that consume scarce bandwidth before being dropped farther along a path. Its analysis concludes that the increased initial window does not create a danger of congestion collapse, though a highly congested network can see higher loss rates and more retransmission timeouts.
sections.plainLanguage: A larger first burst can lose packets when a path is already congested. The RFC's analysis found no congestion-collapse danger, but warns that very congested paths can see more losses.

sections.title: Studies and Measurements
sections.content:
The RFC summarizes experiments and simulations on satellite, modem, and Internet paths. In one satellite study, a four-segment initial window with a 512-byte MSS improved throughput by up to 30%, depending on transfer size.

In tests involving 16 KB transfers to 100 Internet hosts, four-segment windows reduced transfer time by roughly 25% and increased the drop rate by 0.04 segments per transfer. Other studies found slightly higher loss in most cases, with more noticeable effects in very congested networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The reported studies often found shorter transfer times with larger initial windows. They also found that loss can increase, particularly in a highly congested network.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that changing the permitted initial congestion window raises no known new security issues for TCP. It concerns the amount of data TCP may initially send, not a new authentication or encryption mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC identifies no new security issues from the initial-window change. The change concerns TCP congestion behavior.
